title: Apiiro found passwords and keys in 1,122 public copies of the file where Claude Code saves “don’t ask again” approvals, and old copies stay in git history. On 273 real change requests, the best coding agent met 69.9 percent of criteria per task but fully finished 26.4 percent. The FT says Anthropic paid about $3.4 billion for 1.7 gigawatts of gas generators. Gurman says Apple could make Siri more like an agent as early as next year. Nvidia’s board opened an independent investigation after reports that Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.
summary: Apiiro’s research, published 5 November and written up by The Hacker News on 7 November, found 1,122 of 104,185 public copies of Claude Code’s .claude/settings.local.json holding at least one secret, 1,379 in all, because “Yes, and don’t ask again” can save the exact command, password included. Gitleaks and TruffleHog together missed 215 of those files, and Microsoft says attackers now use an agentic framework, ARTEX, to search GitHub for secrets. Co-Design Bench, covered by The Decoder on 8 November, built 273 tasks from real user coding sessions. GPT-6 Astra led ten models, passing 69.9 percent of criteria per task and fully finishing 26.4 percent of tasks, 41.0 percent of multimodal edits and 17.9 percent of repository edits. The Financial Times reported on 8 November that Anthropic bought commitments for 1.7 gigawatts of gas generators from OnePWR Solutions for about $3.4 billion in late September. Anthropic did not comment. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman wrote on 8 November that John Ternus is pushing Craig Federighi to move faster, that third-party app actions for Siri are likely in the spring, and that Apple could make Siri more like an agent as early as next year. Nvidia’s board said on 8 November that independent directors, with outside counsel, will investigate reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, and that it has no reason to believe secrets were compromised.
uncertainty: Apiiro’s counts are its own, from public GitHub searched 1 to 3 November, as reported by The Hacker News and checked by LATENT. Apiiro did not test whether the secrets work. The 734 secrets in older versions and 211 forks are the report’s. Boris Cherny’s reply is as LATENT quoted it from Hacker News. Microsoft’s five minutes is one observed case in its 5 November post. Co-Design Bench is a preprint. The 69.9, 26.4, 75.4, 41.0, 66.7 and 17.9 percent figures and the harness scores are the paper’s, graded by AI judges with a second AI verifier. The task set uses one fixed request per task. The $3.4 billion, 1.7 gigawatts and late September date are the FT’s, as carried by CNBC, citing a person familiar. Reuters could not verify them and Anthropic did not comment. The $500 billion is a September Reuters report as CNBC cited it. The Siri plans are Gurman’s reporting, as The Verge and his own posts give it. Apple has announced none of it. Nvidia’s statement is first-hand. The spy claim is from a US intelligence memo as TechCrunch reported it, and was not checked here. The share drop is Bloomberg’s post.

stories.theme: Apiiro found passwords and keys in 1,122 public copies of Claude Code’s “don’t ask again” file
stories.changed: On Thursday 5 November 2026 the security company Apiiro published research on .claude/settings.local.json, the file where Claude Code saves a command when a user picks “Yes, and don’t ask again.” The Hacker News, writing on 7 November, says the rule can be the exact command, so a password or token typed into it is saved too, in plain text. Apiiro searched public GitHub from 1 to 3 November and found 104,185 copies of the file in 103,617 repositories. About 1.1 percent of them, 1,122 copies, hold at least one secret, 1,379 distinct secrets in all. More than a third open a database directly, including 379 database passwords. Others include 43 SSH logins for public servers, 42 GitHub, GitLab and npm tokens, and 23 AWS keys. Apiiro did not test whether the secrets still work. The Hacker News says one company it notified confirmed its key had been live. Claude Code adds the file to the user’s global git excludes the first time it writes it, but not to the project’s own .gitignore, so that protection stays on one computer. In 539 of 1,105 repositories traced, a commit listing Claude as a co-author changed the file. Older versions of the file hold 734 more secrets, and 211 forks carry the same secrets as the originals. Gitleaks flagged 564 of the 1,122 files, TruffleHog 643, and neither flagged 215. Of 16 coding agents whose documentation Apiiro compared, Claude Code is the only one confirmed to save the full approved command in a project file by default. LATENT, a site that checked the report, says Boris Cherny of the Claude Code team replied on Hacker News on 7 November that Claude Code has not historically scrubbed secrets and that the team is looking into ways to prevent this. Separately, Microsoft Threat Intelligence wrote on 5 November that attackers are using an agentic framework, ARTEX, to search public GitHub for secrets, and that in one case an agent went from that search to taking data out of Azure Key Vault in five minutes.
stories.matters: A click meant to save time can turn a project folder into a password file. Once that file reaches a public repository, deleting it does not help. Old copies stay in history and forks, and attackers now search with agents.
stories.imply: Do not tell a team the fix is to delete the file. The report says rotate first, then clean up. Do not say 1,379 keys were stolen. Apiiro did not test them. Do not assume a scanner will catch them. Two common scanners together missed 215 of the 1,122 files.
uses: Search your GitHub organization for .claude/settings.local.json and .claude/settings.json, including git history where the files were deleted. That is the report’s first step.
Rotate every password, token and key those files ever held before you untrack them with git rm --cached and add the file to the repository’s own .gitignore.
Pass secrets as variables, such as $DB_URL, and approve patterns like Bash(npm run:*) instead of single commands, so a saved rule never holds the secret itself.
stories.example: A platform lead whose team clicks “don’t ask again” daily reads the 7 November write-up. Apiiro found 1,122 public copies of that file holding secrets, and old copies stay in git history. The team rotates first, then adds the file to every repository’s .gitignore.
stories.audience: Anyone who uses Claude Code on real systems, and the security teams who run secret scanning for them.
stories.watch: Whether Anthropic ships a change that scrubs secrets before saving a rule, as Cherny said the team is looking into. Whether other agents’ settings folders turn up in the same searches.

source.title: The Hacker News: Claude Code’s “Don’t Ask Again” file exposes passwords and keys in 1,122 public copies on GitHub, 7 November 2026
source.quote: Removing it from a project does not undo the leak, because older versions stay in git history and in forks of the repository.

stories.theme: On real users’ change requests, the best coding agent fully finished 26.4 percent of tasks
stories.changed: Researchers from Alibaba and several universities posted Co-Design Bench, a benchmark built from real coding sessions, and The Decoder wrote it up on 8 November 2026. The paper says its 273 tasks were picked from 37,463 deduplicated requests across 26,314 real user sessions, favoring requests users had to rephrase or roll back. Each task starts from a working web app and a change request, sometimes with an image, audio, video or document attached, and is graded against 2,331 hidden acceptance criteria written by experts. One AI judge checks the finished app in a browser, and a second challenges every pass, looking for stubs and hardcoded results. Ten model endpoints ran in the same Claude Code harness, with a three hour and 120 turn cap. The strongest, GPT-6 Astra, passed an average of 69.9 percent of criteria per task but fully satisfied only 26.4 percent of tasks, so 73.6 percent kept at least one unmet requirement. On the 100 multimodal editing tasks it passed 75.4 percent of criteria and fully finished 41.0 percent. On the 173 repository editing tasks it passed 66.7 percent and fully finished 17.9 percent. Combined full-pass rates for the next models were 18.3 percent for Opus 5, 16.5 for Qwen3.8-Max, 15.0 for Qwen3.8-27B and 15.8 for Kimi K3. Every model scored lower on repository tasks that mixed three or four kinds of change than on tasks with one or two. In a separate test the same model scored 0.749 or 0.560 on repository tasks depending on the harness. The paper says the task set evaluates one fixed request, with no follow-up from the user, and that its AI judges can make mistakes.
stories.matters: An agent that meets most of a request can still leave something undone on most tasks. Someone has to find the missing piece. The harness, not only the model, changes how often that happens.
stories.imply: Do not read 69.9 percent as the share of jobs done. It is the average share of criteria met per task. The share fully done is 26.4 percent. Do not compare a model across tools without naming the harness. The paper shows it can move the score by 19 points.
uses: When an agent says done, check every acceptance point in the request, not the overall look. The paper’s gap is exactly that: most points met, at least one missed.
Split change requests that mix layout, design, interaction and content into smaller ones. Every model in the paper did worse when a task combined three or four kinds.
If you are choosing a coding agent, test the model and the harness together on your own tasks. The paper says rankings changed when the harness changed.
stories.example: A product manager asked why agent pull requests still need rework reads the 8 November write-up. On 273 real change requests the best model met 69.9 percent of criteria per task but fully finished 26.4 percent. The team adds a checklist review for each request.
stories.audience: Engineering managers who review agent work, and anyone picking a coding agent from a leaderboard.
stories.watch: Whether other labs report on Co-Design Bench. Whether a version with follow-up turns from the user appears. The paper is a preprint.

source.title: arXiv: Co-Design Bench: Multimodal Collaborative Coding Evaluation for Agentic Models, covered by The Decoder on 8 November 2026
source.quote: Under a shared agentic harness, the strongest of ten model endpoints passes an average of 69.9% of criteria per task but fully satisfies only 26.4% of tasks.

stories.theme: Anthropic paid about $3.4 billion for 1.7 gigawatts of gas generators, the FT reports
stories.changed: On Sunday 8 November 2026 the Financial Times reported that Anthropic has struck a deal worth about $3.4 billion to secure gas-fired power generators for data centers. CNBC, carrying the report, says Anthropic bought commitments for 1.7 gigawatts of heavy-duty generators in late September from OnePWR Solutions, an equipment supplier in San Antonio, Texas. It says Anthropic did not buy OnePWR itself and none of its employees moved to Anthropic, but the deal included the engineering and construction capabilities needed to install the generators, citing a person familiar with the matter. Bloomberg posted that the FT described it as the largest known single purchase of power-generation equipment by an AI lab. Reuters could not immediately verify the report, and Anthropic and OnePWR did not respond to requests for comment. CNBC adds that Reuters reported in September that Anthropic expects to spend more than $500 billion over the next 10 years building AI infrastructure. The deal is reported, not announced. The CNBC copy does not say where the generators will run.
stories.matters: Power is now something AI labs buy directly, like chips. For Claude customers, this is about capacity years out, not anything that changes this week.
stories.imply: Do not say Anthropic built a power plant or bought a company. The report says it took over generator commitments and did not acquire OnePWR. Do not treat the $3.4 billion as confirmed. Anthropic did not comment, and Reuters could not verify it.
uses: In a vendor-risk note on Anthropic, put this next to the September figure: Reuters reported plans to spend more than $500 billion over 10 years on AI infrastructure. Mark both as reported.
If your company is weighing on-site power for its own computing, the useful fact is the route: buying another firm’s existing generator orders instead of waiting for new ones.
Keep the date straight. The deal was struck in late September. It became public on 8 November.
stories.example: A CIO asked whether Anthropic can keep up with demand reads the CNBC copy. The FT says Anthropic bought commitments for 1.7 gigawatts of gas generators for about $3.4 billion in late September. Anthropic did not comment, and the CNBC copy does not say where they will run.
stories.audience: Buyers who depend on Claude capacity, and facilities or energy teams watching how AI labs get power.
stories.watch: Whether Anthropic confirms the deal or names the sites. Whether its IPO filing mentions it. Not a new model.

source.title: CNBC: Anthropic secures $3.4 billion generator deal for AI data centers, FT reports, 8 November 2026
source.quote: The AI startup bought commitments for 1.7 gigawatts of heavy-duty generators in late September from OnePWR Solutions, a San Antonio, Texas-based equipment supplier, the report said.

stories.theme: Gurman says Apple could make Siri more like an agent as early as next year. Third-party app actions come first
stories.changed: On Sunday 8 November 2026 Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman wrote in his Power On newsletter that Apple chief executive John Ternus held a closed-door meeting with software chief Craig Federighi in the last few weeks, pushing him to accelerate Apple’s AI road map and move beyond Siri improvements. The Verge, summarizing the report the same day, says two changes are expected in the coming months. With iOS 27.3, Siri is expected to get fine-grained control over Apple’s own apps, such as rotating and cropping images in Photos and organizing Safari tabs. Integration with third-party apps is likely to land later, in the spring, according to Gurman, which would let Siri place an order through Grubhub or book a table through OpenTable. Gurman wrote that Dots, Muse and Grok can keep track of goals and keep pursuing them without the user starting every step, that Apple ultimately wants to go in that direction, and that he believes Apple could make Siri more like an agent as early as next year. In a separate post he said Mike Rockwell, who leads Siri, continues to seriously consider leaving that role or Apple next year. Apple has not announced any of this.
stories.matters: Siri acting inside other companies’ apps is the step that matters for anyone with an iPhone app. An agent that keeps working on a goal is still a report, not a product.
stories.imply: Do not tell anyone Siri will be an agent in 2027. Gurman says as early as next year, based on what he was told. Do not promise third-party actions on a date. The Verge says likely in the spring.
uses: If you own an iPhone app, list the two or three actions customers would ask Siri to do, such as order or book. That is the kind of integration the report expects in the spring.
If you plan device rollouts, treat iOS 27.3’s control of Apple’s own apps as the near-term change. Photos and Safari are the examples given.
When someone compares Siri with ChatGPT Dots or Meta Muse, quote Gurman’s line: Apple wants to go in that direction, as early as next year.
stories.example: A mobile lead asked whether to prepare for Siri ordering through their app reads the 8 November Verge piece. Third-party app integration is likely in the spring, says Gurman. A more agentic Siri could come as early as next year. Apple has not confirmed either.
stories.audience: Teams that build iPhone apps, and IT staff who plan Apple device updates.
stories.watch: What ships in iOS 27.3. Whether third-party app actions arrive in the spring. Whether Rockwell stays. Not a new model.

source.title: The Verge: Apple is racing to make Siri more agentic, 8 November 2026
source.quote: The bigger change, integration with third-party apps, is likely to land later, in the Spring, according to Gurman.

stories.theme: Nvidia’s board opened an independent investigation after reports that Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort
stories.changed: On Sunday 8 November 2026 Nvidia’s board said it is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and chief executive Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee it. The board said it has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry will examine all available information. It said Huang fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating, and that the board has confidence in him and his leadership team. CNBC published a staff email from Huang the same day in which he apologized for being unfaithful to his wife, said he supports the investigation and will cooperate fully, and said he is fully committed to Nvidia. CNBC reported that Nvidia told it Huang is committed to continuing to lead the company as chief executive without interruption. TechCrunch has reported that a US intelligence memo claimed a Megaspeed executive was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Huang. On Monday Bloomberg posted that Nvidia shares dropped after the board launched the investigation. The investigation has no stated end date, and the board said it will provide further updates as appropriate.
stories.matters: Nvidia supplies most of the chips AI runs on, so its leadership is a supply question for many companies. For now the board says it has no reason to think secrets were compromised.
stories.imply: Do not write that Nvidia secrets leaked. The board says it has no reason to believe that. Do not say Huang is stepping down. The company says he will continue to lead without interruption. Keep the spy claims attributed to the reports.
uses: If you keep a supplier-risk register, add one line: Nvidia board investigation opened 8 November, led by independent directors with outside counsel, no finding yet.
Quote the board’s statement, not the headlines, in any internal note. It is short and it is the only first-hand account of what is being examined.
If you have chip orders in progress, nothing in the statement changes them. Watch the board’s next update instead.
stories.example: A procurement lead asked whether the Nvidia news affects a GPU order reads the board’s 8 November statement. An independent committee will investigate, the board sees no sign secrets were compromised, and Huang continues as chief executive. The order stands while the review runs.
stories.audience: Procurement and risk teams that depend on Nvidia hardware, and anyone briefing leadership on AI suppliers.
stories.watch: The board’s next update and any findings. Whether US officials comment. Not a new model.
